name: Nora Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. This conversation is confidential. What did you work on today?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was on care-home accounts this morning, asking why three supplier invoices had the same number but different dates. I'm 43, a mid-level accountant at Willow Ledger; I have a bachelor's degree and a professional accountancy qualification, and my work is decent rather than remarkable. I like when the care manager can understand what is left for wages; I dislike chasing a signed receipt while the tax deadline keeps moving closer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And when you go home, what are you balancing there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Tomas cooks at a hotel, and our children are six and twelve. We have a mortgage, my accounting pay is low for this kind of work, less than one month of expenses saved and few similar firms nearby. I use AI now and then for a first draft after another accountant has tested it, but I verify invoice numbers against the originals. I usually look for a workable middle ground: what costs, what helps and who is responsible if it fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a small invoice sorter could help if we keep the original bill beside it. The care manager deserves an answer they can check, not a quick number with no trail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect Willow Ledger to keep my role, but Tomas's hotel shifts vary and our mortgage account is too close to empty. Less than one month saved means I already worry about a missed weekend at the hotel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking care-home invoices against the originals and use AI only for drafts I can verify. Starting this month we'd cancel one paid television package and add thirty-five a month to the mortgage buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the household budget, even if AI barely changes. One cancelled hotel weekend can take away the margin we had for groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who notices the cut at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children mostly notice when we say no to a new game. Tomas and I can live without another television package, and the mortgage needs the money more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for a new AI tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not before a colleague tests it on old invoices and shows the errors. I don't mind a tool that works, but I won't call an untested figure an account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Willow Ledger to test the system on last year's care-home files and give staff the error count. If checking and letters get faster, the new rota should be explained before anyone loses a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those checking and writing tasks are most of my work, and I expect my paid week to lose a day before the partners decide what else to sell. I'm an average accountant and not hard to replace, so the mortgage would feel that cut quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a paid afternoon with the senior to test eight closed care-home files and learn the system's mistakes. In the first year of steady change, if my pay falls, I'd apply for the posted accounts vacancy at the care-home group only if it still exists, while keeping my funded Willow Ledger hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect a real pay cut, not just more work. Tomas's variable shifts cannot fill the gap on a mortgage week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm won't fund a test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my current checking routine and ask for the staffing decision in writing. I would not upload a care resident's bill to an unapproved tool at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the care-home job usable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written salary and start date covering the mortgage, with shifts that leave one of us free for our younger child's school pickup. I would not resign for a vacancy notice alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team full AGI in 2028 reaches accounts and tax returns, so we should see the firm's fees and staffing dates now. The care homes should know who remains responsible for their reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The 2028 date hits my desk, while robots arrive around 2031 for hands-on work like some of Tomas's hotel tasks. I expect my accounting hours to fall sharply, and our mortgage cannot live on his uncertain shifts alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd pause the children's paid dance class for a term and put its fifty-five monthly fee into the mortgage buffer. In the first year after 2028, if Willow Ledger ends my job, I'd apply for posted salaried supplier-payments work at the hospital and request income support if eligible while keeping any paid work the firm still has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. The household may have only weeks of cash when the next loan payment arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about dance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we are practising at home until the buffer holds one mortgage payment. I would ask the teacher for the free community session so they still see their friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an unpaid hospital trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I need the hours paid and a named vacancy with a salary range and start date. A trial without those is not a job I can put in our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets the care-home group decide whether it needs a person to handle supplier payment problems. I would like a straight answer on paid posts, not a general promise to adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031 I would still have children and a mortgage, and AGI can check invoices faster than I can. Tomas's hands-on hotel work may face robots around 2034, so we need the years before then to build cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the hospital's payments office about a funded part-time accounting post next year and ask Willow Ledger to keep my current wage if I train there. In the first year after 2031, if my firm cuts my salary and an actual hospital post is advertised, I'd apply for it; without a funded place, I'd stay on my paid care-home accounts and save thirty-five monthly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but five years could let me test another paid desk before the accounts fees fall. I cannot afford a course with no wage attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the payments office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd trace a supplier's late payment from invoice entry to bank transfer, with a supervisor checking my first cases. I would take the part-time post only if the hours and pay are written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Willow Ledger won't protect your salary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not take the part-time post unless the hospital wage replaces what I lose and covers the mortgage. I'd keep my present paid accounts work while I wait for a real vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us time to lower the mortgage and see which work the firm can still pay for. The answer may be different for the hospital and for our small care-home clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036 I would still need work even if the children have finished school. AGI reaches my desk then, and robots around 2039 may change Tomas's kitchen work later; saving now helps both dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put an extra ninety monthly against mortgage principal while both wages hold and ask Willow Ledger to let me lead paid monthly supplier-payment checks for three care homes. In the first year after 2036, if at least two homes renew at fees covering my salary, I'd stay; if not, I'd apply for posted salaried hospital finance jobs and keep any funded firm hours until a written wage offer starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious. A smaller mortgage still needs income at 53. Ten years lets me count real renewals before relying on a service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show the care manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Which supplier payments are late and whether a duplicate invoice is waiting in the queue. If the manager will not pay for another month, we stop calling it a service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for your own software to do this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the checks are Willow Ledger work and the client fees belong to the firm. I would keep my household savings for bills if the office later shrinks.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a fast hours cut could arrive before we have even one mortgage payment saved. A dated hours plan, a real paid hospital vacancy and help covering the gap would matter. I can check an invoice twice; I cannot make a late wage arrive sooner.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who calls a care manager when a computer approves the same supplier bill twice. The bill does not disappear because the screen looked confident.

headlineQuote: I can check an invoice twice; I cannot make a late wage arrive sooner.
portrait: Nora, **43**, is an average-skilled mid-level accountant at Willow Ledger with a bachelor’s degree and professional qualification.
Her **low pay**, under-one-month savings and few nearby firms put a mortgage and two school-age children close to risk.
She uses AI **occasionally after colleagues** and checks care-home invoices against the original paper.
She fears **2028 hours cuts** most, then seeks funded hospital work and tests a paid care-home service.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut her hours before the family saves one mortgage payment.
whatWouldHelp: A **dated hours plan**, paid hospital vacancy and temporary gap help would matter.
